title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Stock Trades Here — Market Expectations vs. Peers

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. When a market-cap giant trades at forty-four times trailing earnings, the real question is not whether the multiple looks high—it is what cash-flow trajectory that price already demands.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Desk

web_blocks.html: At the November 18, 2026 close of $1,382.75, Eli Lilly holds a market cap of $1,274.30 billion and an enterprise value of $1,319.94 billion. That reflects ~$42.5 billion of gross debt from its >$50 billion U.S. plant buildout, minus ~$5.19 per share in cash [2, 18]. On trailing twelve-month (TTM) results, Lilly earned $86.46 billion in sales, a 51.25% operating margin, and $27.58 billion in net income ($30.44 TTM EPS). At $1,382.75, the stock trades at 44.54x trailing P/E, 15.27x EV/Sales, and 28.39x EV/EBITDA [4, 18].

Trailing multiples always lag fast-growing drug platforms. Looking forward, Lilly raised FY2026 sales guidance to $91.0B–$92.0B and Non-GAAP EPS to $35.00–$36.00, even after $4.57/share of Q3 acquired IPR&D charges [4]. Consensus estimates bring LLY's Forward P/E down to 26.75x against a 33.76% 5-year EPS CAGR, giving a PEG ratio of 0.79. In plain terms, the market no longer pays a hype premium. It prices Lilly below its medium-term earnings growth rate, while still demanding steady volume, net pricing, and future FCF gains.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF Implied Expectations at $1,382.75 CMP ($1,319.94B Enterprise Value)
rows: Requires incretin TAM + Foundayo/retatrutide expansion to offset -10% to -15% annual net price erosion
TTM EBIT margin is already 51.25%; 44% allows 725 bps of pricing/mix cushion

web_blocks.takeaway: To justify $1,382.75 today, Lilly does not need miracle assumptions—it needs ~13.8% 10-year revenue compounding and ~29.5% terminal FCF margins as its $50B+ manufacturing buildout matures.

web_blocks.html: Breaking down the Reverse DCF shows why investors are both impressed and careful. In FY2025, Lilly generated $16,813 million in operating cash flow and spent $7,841 million on plants and equipment. That left $8,972 million in free cash flow, or a 64.87x trailing P/FCF multiple [3]. Why is P/FCF so much higher than Forward P/E (26.75x)? Lilly is spending over $50 billion up front to build sterile fill-finish and peptide API plants ahead of demand. As those plants shift from construction to full output between 2027 and 2029, growth capex will taper. That shift should lift free cash flow conversion toward 75%–85% of net income.

web_blocks.text: Decision Trigger: A weekly close below $1,158.45 (breaking the 30-week SMA at $1,180.13) or realized net price declines deepening past -20% YoY without offsetting +35% volume growth would invalidate the Base $1,660.00 valuation thesis.

web_blocks.caption: Head-to-Head Peer Valuation & Quality Comparison (2026-11-18 Market Close)
web_blocks.takeaway: LLY trades at a clear valuation premium to legacy pharma (NVO at 11.4x Fwd P/E, PFE at 9.4x, MRK at 14.9x) and closer to high-moat biotech (VRTX at 26.3x), justified by 45.5% TTM sales growth and 31.6% ROIC.

web_blocks.mechanism: As the incumbent GLP-1 pioneer (Ozempic/Wegovy), Novo Nordisk commanded >40x forward earnings at peak 2024 optimism before supply bottlenecks, CagriSema clinical disappointment relative to tirzepatide, and aggressive U.S. net price concessions compressed its multiple to 11.44x Forward P/E and 5.19x EV/EBITDA in Stage 4 downtrend.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: NVO sits at $39.43 ($130.0B market cap, 9.79x trailing P/E, 5.19x EV/EBITDA) vs. LLY's $1,274.3B market cap and 26.75x Forward P/E—an ~10x valuation spread for the same incretin duopoly.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Novo Nordisk's de-rating proves that even in a secular obesity boom, losing clinical efficacy leadership or stumbling on net-price vs. volume math triggers brutal multiple compression. LLY earns its premium only as long as tirzepatide, Foundayo, and retatrutide defend clinical superiority and +50% volume growth outpaces -15% realized price erosion.

web_blocks.title: Valuation Synthesis Against Pass 1 Business Quality
paragraphs: Pass 1 graded Eli Lilly COMPOUNDER_PASS with PASS on all 6 leading KPIs. At 26.75x Forward P/E and 0.79x PEG, the market is pricing LLY as a durable compounder rather than a bubble—leaving ~20.05% upside to our $1,660 Base fair value if 2027–2028 oral (Foundayo) and triple-agonist (retatrutide) launches convert capex into FCF.

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have completed our price-blind audit of Eli Lilly's business engine—and graded it a clear Compounder Pass—we are finally allowed to look at the price tag. As of the November 18, 2026 close, Lilly changes hands at $1,382.75 per share, valuing the enterprise at roughly $1.32 trillion.

On the surface, 44.54 times trailing earnings and 28.39 times EV/EBITDA look demanding. Any value investor trained on 15x-earnings industrial stocks would flinch. But look one line deeper at what the business is actually doing right now: trailing twelve-month revenue has reached $86.46 billion, operating margins sit at 51.25%, and management just raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $91.0–$92.0 billion with Non-GAAP EPS of $35.00–$36.00.

When you divide today's share price by next year's expected earnings, that 44.5x trailing multiple collapses to 26.75x Forward P/E. Against a consensus five-year EPS growth rate of 33.76%, Lilly trades at a PEG ratio of 0.79. You are paying less than one unit of valuation multiple for each unit of expected earnings growth—for a company generating a 31.61% return on invested capital.

book_subsections.title: What the Reverse DCF Demands (And Why CapEx Distorts Trailing FCF)
paragraphs: Rather than guessing a target multiple out of thin air, let's invert the question: what must Eli Lilly deliver over the next decade for a buyer at $1,382.75 to earn an 8.5% hurdle rate? Using our Reverse DCF model, the current $1.32 trillion enterprise value implies roughly a 13.8% ten-year revenue CAGR (scaling from ~$91.5 billion in 2026 toward ~$333 billion by 2035) alongside a 29.5% terminal free cash flow margin.

Notice why trailing Price-to-Free-Cash-Flow looks elevated at 64.87x: in FY2025, Lilly plowed $7.84 billion into property, plant, and equipment out of $16.81 billion in operating cash flow, leaving $8.97 billion in free cash flow. That capital expenditure is not maintenance spending to keep the lights on; it is the upfront construction cost of more than $50 billion in U.S. sterile fill-finish and peptide synthesis capacity. Once those plants come online and capex normalizes from ~12% of sales back toward 6%–7%, free cash flow conversion should snap back toward 75%–85% of net income.

book_subsections.title: The Peer Reality Check: Why LLY Trades at 26.8x While Novo Nordisk Trades at 11.4x
paragraphs: Look across the major biopharma peer table and one contrast jumps off the page. Novo Nordisk—Lilly's direct duopoly rival in GLP-1 medicines—trades at just 11.44x Forward P/E and 5.19x EV/EBITDA in a Stage 4 downtrend. Meanwhile, Merck trades at 14.93x Forward P/E ahead of its Keytruda cliff, Pfizer sits at 9.37x, Amgen at 17.59x, and Vertex—the closest high-moat specialty peer—trades at 26.25x Forward P/E.

Why does the market award Lilly more than double Novo Nordisk's forward multiple? Because clinical efficacy, oral pipeline execution (Foundayo), and supply-chain reliability broke in Lilly's favor. In Q3 2026, Lilly grew volume by 53%, easily absorbing a 15% realized price decline. Novo Nordisk's de-rating is a live warning for us, though: if Lilly ever loses clinical leadership or allows net price erosion to outrun volume, its multiple has plenty of room to compress.

book_subsections.title: Sensitivity to Net Price Erosion and Post-CapEx Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: Let us stress-test the two levers that matter most in our Reverse DCF: annual net price realization and capital-expenditure normalization. In Q3 2026, Lilly absorbed a 15% year-over-year decline in realized net prices across its U.S. incretin portfolio while growing total unit volume by 53%. As long as unit volume outpaces price concessions by more than three-to-one, revenue and operating dollars continue to compound rapidly, because incremental gross margins on peptide and small-molecule manufacturing sit above 80%.

Where could that math break? Look at our Bear Case ($1,040.00): if Medicare negotiations, commercial PBM rebating, and competitive launches from Novo Nordisk, Amgen's MariTide, or Roche push annual net price erosion above 20% while volume growth decelerates into the teens, Lilly's 10-year revenue CAGR would settle closer to 9.5% rather than 13.8%. At 36% steady-state EBIT margins and a compressed 20x forward multiple, the stock would re-rate toward $1,040—a 24.79% drawdown from $1,382.75. Conversely, if Foundayo captures needle-averse primary-care patients globally and retatrutide delivers superior weight-loss durability upon its Q1 2027 BLA filing, Lilly can compound at 16.5% annually with 33% terminal free cash flow margins, supporting our $1,920.00 Bull Case.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The biggest mistake investors make with capital-intensive compounders is confusing growth capex with poor cash conversion. Lilly's 64.9x trailing P/FCF is a photograph of a company mid-construction; its 26.8x Forward P/E and 0.79 PEG are the movie of what happens when those factories start shipping.
